root_motivation: Every call, meter tick, signup, and event is a row that stays forever: grep -rniE 'retention|prune|vacuum|purge' src migrations finds only host.runs.purge (handler.rs:824) and the deploy-time VACUUM INTO. On a ccx13 with one disk shared with the site and the hub, that is a slow outage with a known date -- a 25,000-call stress run (PRD-mcphost-call-limits-honest) wrote 25,000 calls rows in minutes, and a synthetic panel run per hour writes hundreds of rows an hour with no ceiling. The 09-12 decision set 30-day access-log retention and the database has none. This PRD is a proactive capacity fix pulled forward from a vision addendum (2026-09-18, leaf 2), not a failure investigation: it adds a per-table retention policy with billing-safe defaults, a nightly in-process prune, database size and per-table row counts in admin.usage, and a disk guard that refuses writes before the box fills.
user_persona: Two: (1) the operator (Joe), who today cannot say how large the database is or when the disk fills -- sets $MCPHOST_RETENTION_CALLS_DAYS and reads admin.usage/healthz to watch db_bytes stay flat and the nightly prune's last_prune_ok/deleted counts, and gets a clear service_unavailable instead of a corrupted file when disk runs out; (2) a tenant, who still sees their own last 30 days in host.usage after a prune, and can read their own retention windows there.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given `calls` rows aged 91 and 89 days and `MCPHOST_RETENTION_CALLS_DAYS=90`, When the prune runs, Then the 91-day row is deleted and the 89-day row remains.
Given metering rows 399 days old, When the prune runs, Then none is deleted.
Given a table not in the policy, When the prune runs, Then its row count is unchanged.
Given 20,000 expired rows, When the prune runs, Then it deletes in batches and no concurrent `host.tool_call` fails with `database is locked`.
Given a completed prune, When `admin.usage` is read, Then `rows_by_table`, `db_bytes`, and `last_prune.deleted` are present and consistent with the deletion.
Given free space below the floor (simulated by a test hook), When `host.tool_call` runs, Then it returns `service_unavailable: disk floor` and `healthz` reports `disk_ok: false`.
Given prod after ship, When `admin.usage` is read on the following day, Then `last_prune` is younger than 24 h (proof: the live read in the trailer).
acceptance_criteria.test: deferred -- prod-only proof, no branch-local test possible before ship; see PRD frontmatter mock_justifications and agent/test-map.json's ac_test_map.AC7

acceptance_criteria.description: Given a tenant, When `host.usage` is called, Then the retention windows are listed.
Given a prune that errors, When `healthz` is read, Then `last_prune_ok` is false.
Given admin scope, When `admin.prune_now` is called, Then one cycle runs and returns its counts.

scope: `migrations/0026_retention.sql` (new): `retention_policy(table_name, days, updated_unix)` and `prune_log(id, started_unix, finished_unix, ok, error, deleted_json)`, plus a one-time `auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL` pragma switch + `VACUUM` rebuild (requirement 2's own 'set before the first table exists' rule, applied late via a one-time VACUUM since 25 prior migrations already created tables).

`src/retention.rs` (new): the per-table policy registry (`POLICY_TABLES`, requirement 1's 8 tables and their env-configurable defaults), the executable-table registry mapping each policy entry to its physical table/age-column/extra-WHERE, the batched (5,000-row) `rowid IN (SELECT ... LIMIT ...)` delete loop run on its own dedicated SQLite connection with its own `busy_timeout` (technical considerations: 'must not hold the write lock longer than busy_timeout per batch'), the nightly scheduler (`spawn_prune_scheduler`, 03:30 UTC jittered up to 10 minutes), and `DiskGuard` (requirement 4's write-floor check, a real `statvfs(2)` probe with a test-only override).

`src/db.rs`: `Db::open` gains its own `busy_timeout` (so the shared app connection and the prune's dedicated one genuinely contend for SQLite's write lock, AC4); `Db::seed_retention_policy_from_env`/`retention_windows`/`prune_once`/`usage_size_stats`/`last_prune_ok` plus their `PruneReport`/`UsageSizeStats`/`LastPrune` return shapes and a handful of `_for_test` fixture helpers (bulk calls-row insert, meter-event-row insert, arbitrary-table row count, retention-days override in place of a racy process env var).
`src/admin.rs`/`src/handler.rs`: `admin.usage` gains `db_bytes`/`db_page_free_bytes`/`rows_by_table`/`last_prune`; a new `admin.prune_now` tool (P2, AC10) runs one cycle on demand.

`src/control.rs`/`src/errors.rs`/`src/http.rs`: `host.usage` gains `retention_days`; `AppError::disk_floor` (code `service_unavailable`) gates `host_tool_call`/`tool_publish`/`signup`; `/healthz` gains `disk_ok` (folded into the anonymous `ok`/503, AC14 precedent) and `last_prune_ok`.

`src/main.rs`/`src/state.rs`/`src/tables.rs`/`tests/common/mod.rs`: `AppState.disk_guard`, `seed_retention_policy_from_env()` called once after `migrate()`, and `spawn_prune_scheduler` started alongside the existing runs-executor/scheduler-tick background tasks.
non_goals: No archiving pruned rows off-box -- the backup PRD keeps daily copies (PRD's own Non-goals).
No change to tenant quotas (PRD's own Non-goals).
No per-table retention window configurable via an MCP tool -- only via `$MCPHOST_RETENTION_<TABLE>_DAYS` at process start (requirement 1); a future PRD could add an `admin.retention_set` tool.
No archiving/undo for a pruned row -- deletion is permanent; the PRD's success metric treats this as intentional (flat db size over time), not a gap.

No separate `calls_resource_usage` physical table -- migration 0004 added `cpu_ms`/`peak_rss_kb` as extra nullable columns on `calls` itself, not a second table; its own env-configurable window is tracked in `retention_policy` purely for observability/operator-configurability, since pruning `calls` by the `calls` window already removes those columns' rows.

additional.no_new_dependency_for_disk_stat: The disk-floor probe uses `libc::statvfs` (already a dependency, used elsewhere for sandbox rlimits) rather than adding a `fs2`/`sysinfo`-class crate for one syscall.
additional.prune_on_its_own_connection: The prune's batched deletes run on a freshly-opened `rusqlite::Connection` to the same file, not `Db`'s shared `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>` -- so it and the app's own writes are two real SQLite connections genuinely contending for the single write lock (the scenario `busy_timeout`, not an in-process mutex, exists to cover), matching the technical considerations' 'must not hold the write lock longer than busy_timeout per batch'.
additional.batch_size_5000: Deletes run in batches of exactly 5,000 rows per requirement 2, via a `rowid IN (SELECT rowid ... LIMIT 5000)` shape rather than `DELETE ... LIMIT` (this crate's bundled `rusqlite`/`libsqlite3-sys` build does not enable `SQLITE_ENABLE_UPDATE_DELETE_LIMIT`).
additional.auto_vacuum_incremental_via_one_time_vac: `PRAGMA auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL` only takes effect on a fresh database; migration 0026 runs 26th, so it pairs the pragma with a one-time `VACUUM` (gated by the same idempotency check as the migration's own table creation) to actually rebuild every already-deployed database under the new mode, per the PRD's own 'startup cost noted in the changelog' framing.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does Joe worry the mcphost box will run out of disk?
five_whys_trace.a: Every append-only table (calls, events/event_dedupe, signup_events, meter_events, runs, threads/messages) has grown since its own migration with no purge and no size instrumentation -- grep for retention/prune/vacuum/purge across src and migrations finds only the tenant-driven host.runs.purge.

five_whys_trace.q: Why did no earlier migration add a purge for its own table?
five_whys_trace.a: Each table's migration was scoped to the feature that needed it (billing, metering, scheduling, messaging), not to that table's long-run lifecycle -- no PRD before this one made retention a P0 requirement.

five_whys_trace.q: Why did that gap stay invisible long enough to need a dedicated PRD now?
five_whys_trace.a: The cost only became concrete under load: PRD-mcphost-call-limits-honest's stress run wrote 25,000 calls rows in minutes, and a synthetic panel now runs hourly, writing hundreds of rows an hour with no ceiling.

five_whys_trace.q: Why is that growth dangerous specifically on this box?
five_whys_trace.a: The database's disk (a ccx13) is shared with the site and the hub -- unbounded row growth is not just wasted space, it is a slow outage with a knowable date once free space crosses zero.

five_whys_trace.q: Why is a per-table policy plus a disk guard the right fix, not just a bigger disk?
five_whys_trace.a: A bigger disk delays the same unbounded-growth failure without bounding it, and still corrupts the file if it fills mid-write; a policy table plus a floor that fails closed (service_unavailable) fixes the growth rate and the failure mode at once, and gives every future table's migration one retention_policy row to add instead of its own purge logic.
